The manager bounce effect is a statistical artifact arising from regression to the mean and contextual confounders. It manifests as a temporary spike in performance immediately following a managerial change, but dissipates rapidly upon adjustment for fixture difficulty and team strength. The core insight lies in decomposing this effect into two components: immediate variance and long-term convergence. The former is captured by a short-term cumulative surprise metric, while the latter is modeled through a sequence of tactical identity vectors. These vectors are constructed from micro-metrics such as pressing line height, directness, compactness, and attack speed. Each vector represents a manager’s tactical fingerprint at a given moment. A Bayesian framework allows us to update beliefs about identity convergence over time, incorporating prior knowledge of team structure and opponent strength. The identity fingerprint serves as a proxy for tactical continuity, enabling comparison before and after managerial transitions. Contextual adjustment ensures that performance differences are not attributed to chance or bias. The failure mode occurs when the dataset lacks sufficient bounce events or when micro-metrics fail to distinguish between managers. To mitigate this, we apply a kernel smoothing technique that weights recent observations more heavily, capturing the rapidity of tactical adaptation. This approach enables GSI to forecast manager impact and GSE to simulate tactical evolution under varying regimes.
